headings.title: Introduction to Food Safety and Hygiene in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Food safety and hygiene are foundational pillars of primary health care in Nigeria. Every year, unsafe food causes millions of cases of gastrointestinal illness, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations like children under five and pregnant women. In primary health care settings, nurses frequently encounter patients suffering from preventable foodborne infections. Understanding the journey of food from the farm to the plate allows health workers to identify critical control points where contamination happens. Preventing foodborne disease reduces hospital admissions and lightens the financial burden on families struggling with out-of-pocket health expenses.

headings.title: Key Principles of Food Hygiene
headings.content:
Food hygiene relies on specific actions that prevent harmful microorganisms from contaminating food items. Contamination can be biological, chemical, or physical. 

- **Cleaning**: Regularly washing hands, utensils, and work surfaces with soap and clean water removes visible dirt and invisible microbes.
- **Separating**: Keeping raw meat, poultry, and seafood away from ready-to-eat foods stops cross-contamination.
- **Cooking**: Heating food to the proper internal temperature kills most pathogenic bacteria and parasites.
- **Chilling**: Promptly refrigerating perishable foods slows down the rapid multiplication of bacteria at room temperature.

headings.title: Common Foodborne Pathogens in Nigeria
headings.content:
Foodborne illnesses in Nigeria stem from various bacterial, viral, and parasitic agents often spread through contaminated water, unhygienic food handling, or improper storage.

- **Salmonella species**: Commonly found in poultry, eggs, and unpasteurized milk, causing severe enteric fever and diarrhea.
- **Escherichia coli (E. coli)**: Often linked to faecal contamination of water sources and unwashed vegetables.
- **Cholera (Vibrio cholerae)**: Associated with poor sanitation and contaminated drinking water, leading to rapid, fatal dehydration.
- **Parasites**: Organisms like Taenia solium spread through inadequately cooked pork or beef.

headings.title: Safe Food Handling, Preparation, and Storage
headings.content: Safe food handling practices protect consumers at home, in markets, and in commercial food establishments. Hand hygiene remains the single most effective barrier against microbial transfer; hands must be washed with soap before touching food and after using the toilet. Food handlers with open skin lesions, boils, or respiratory symptoms must be restricted from food preparation areas to avoid introducing Staphylococcus aureus or other pathogens. Storage practices require maintaining refrigerators below 4 degrees Celsius and hot foods above 60 degrees Celsius to keep food out of the temperature danger zone.

headings.title: Water Safety and Sanitation in Food Processing
headings.content: Water is both an ingredient in food preparation and a cleansing agent for utensils and raw produce. Using contaminated water instantly defeats other hygiene measures, spreading pathogens to large volumes of food. Community water sources must be protected from agricultural runoff and sewage contamination. When piped treated water is unavailable, boiling, chlorination, or filtration provides safe water for washing vegetables and preparing meals. Proper waste disposal and sanitary latrines located away from food preparation sites prevent flies and other vectors from carrying filth to edible items.

headings.title: Community Health Education and Promotion
headings.content: Nurses play a vital role in educating communities about safe food practices through market outreaches, antenatal clinics, and school health programs. Effective education respects local culinary traditions while gently correcting dangerous habits like leaving cooked stews at room temperature overnight. Health messaging must be practical, utilizing local languages and visual aids for illiterate community members. Engaging local food vendors, market leaders, and restaurant owners creates lasting behavioral change and improves public health standards across the entire neighborhood.
